title: Three Plays Left
passages:
The Marrow groaned in her lines, hull kissing the Kettle's concrete flank with every swell. Storm bell hammered from the arcology's crown — three strikes, pause, three strikes — and the channel current ran thick with debris: broken pallets, a shipping container's corner, the bloated white of something that had once been a dog. Tide marks on the gate's steel ribs showed maybe forty minutes before the lock teeth engaged and the Stair drowned for the season.

Wren sat in the cabin's aft corner, slate cradled in both hands. Salt crust feathered its edges. The recorder's housing had flooded at forty-two meters, pressure forcing brine through every seal, and the works whined when she tilted it — a sound like a dying insect. Salas sat opposite, berth book open on his knees, pen frozen mid-stroke. He hadn't spoken since they'd surfaced. Fourteen months in an air pocket had hollowed him to a thing that breathed and watched and waited.

"Three plays," Wren said, not looking up. "Maybe two if the salt's eaten the second head. After that it's brick." She thumbed the contact clean on her sleeve, pressed the actuator. "Everyone who needs to hear this, get in here."

Dey appeared in the companionway first, scrubber harness dangling from one hand, the other braced against the frame. His chest rattled — wet, deep, the sound of lungs that had traded their last clean air for a boy named Teo. Nia slipped in behind him, Teo tucked against her hip, the boy's fingers knotted in her shirt. Bayo leaned in the hatch, bandaged hands tucked into his armpits, calling the surge timing to Sol up on deck. Sol came last, rain-slick oilskin dripping on the deck plates, eyes moving from Wren to Salas to the slate and back.

"Play it," Sol said.

The speaker crackled. Static swallowed the cabin, thick and wet. The crew leaned in.

The static thinned into something with a shape.

Water first — the hollow roar of a flooded stairwell, and under it the tick of a depth gauge counting up. A diver's breath, slow and metered, gas hissing through a regulator. Every few seconds a thud came through the housing, and Wren put a finger on the slate's speaker to feel it: a heartbeat, recorded off somebody's chest strap fourteen months ago and still going, patient as a metronome.

The picture came up gray and grainy, a lamp cone swinging across a wall of silt. A door frame drifted past. Then a woman's voice, close to the mic and completely calm.

"Vos to the line. Leave the pharmacy. It's stripped, we took all of it, stop pulling at it."

Dey snorted. "Even drowned she's telling people to stop wasting air."

Nia didn't laugh. She had gone very still against the bulkhead, Teo's weight settled on her hip, her eyes fixed on the slate like it might bite.

On the recording, metal groaned — a hatch dog spinning loose, three quarter-turns, the sound every diver on the coast knows in their teeth. Mara's voice again, unhurried, the way you'd talk to someone standing next to you on a dock instead of forty meters down in the dark.

"Salas, hold at the seal. Don't come past me. There's a second hatch under this deck, service side, and it's not on the hospital plans. Sealed from the inside. I've been keeping the Caller lit so somebody would come and open it."

Across the cabin, Salas's pen did not move. His eyes were on the book in his lap, on a line of his own handwriting he had not finished, and he gave the recording nothing at all.

"Second seal is four meters down the trunk from the pharmacy hatch," Mara said. "Past the Line, so plan your gas and plan who's coming back up. Don't send anyone down there who's already been hollowed once."

"Comforting," Bayo said from the hatch. His bandaged hands were still in his armpits. "She's got a real gift for it."

"Past the Line the cold gets in your head and takes hours out of you," Wren said, to nobody, because everyone in the room already knew it and she needed to hear it said out loud in her own voice. "They don't come back."

She knew that voice better than she knew her own handwriting. She had gone down after Mara Vos and come up with fifty-two minutes missing, and in the middle of those minutes there had been a woman calling her name up out of the black, patient, over and over, the way you call a dog home in weather. Wren had traded away eleven seconds of her own recorded voice to give that woman her voice back. Now here it was again, coming out of a dead man's slate, fourteen months old, telling strangers how to do a job.

"You've got the big drum on the Marrow," Mara said on the tape. "Rig it. Don't send a child."

Nia made a small sound. Teo patted her arm with a hand that had a needle bruise in it.

The lamp cone swung down. Silt, then a flat gray expanse of deck plate, then the shadow of a hatch coaming with the hospital's service stencil half-eaten by rust. The diver's breathing went shallow and quick, and the heartbeat in the housing picked up, and Mara's voice stayed level through all of it, reading numbers off a gauge the way another woman might read a shopping list.

"Depth on my gauge," she said, "is sixty-one meters."

The tape hissed. Somebody on the recording said something that the salt had eaten. The gauge ticked twice more, and the lamp went out, and there was only the roar of the stairwell and that patient thudding heart.

Nobody in the cabin said anything.

Dey's mouth was open. Bayo had stopped calling the surge. Nia's hand had closed on Teo's shirt, and Sol stood in the doorway with rain running off her oilskin onto the deck plates, absolutely motionless, looking at the slate as if it had spoken her name instead of Mara's.

Outside, the storm bell hammered three strikes and paused, and the pause went on longer than the count.

The tape died to white noise. Wren let the actuator click back, the small mechanical sound too loud in the cabin. Two plays left. The salt had not eaten the second head yet.

She set the slate on the chart table, careful of the wet rings. Her fingers moved on the housing — wiping salt from the contacts, checking the spool tension, the readout window fogged but still legible. *Two. Good. Two is workable.*

"Sixty-one meters," Dey said. His voice came out thin, reedy. He cleared his throat and tried again. "Sixty-one. That's — that's past the pharmacy pocket by, what, eighteen meters? Nineteen?"

"Twenty-two," Wren said. She didn't look up from the slate. "Pharmacy hatch sits at thirty-nine. Service trunk drops another twenty-two to the second seal. Past the Line by twelve meters at least. Maybe more if the silt's shifted."

"Twelve meters past the Line," Bayo repeated. He'd pulled his hands from his armpits, bandages white-knuckled against the hatch frame. "That's not a dive. That's a funeral with extra steps."

"Mara did it," Nia said. Quiet. Teo's head rested on her shoulder, eyes closed, but his fingers still moved on her shirt. "She went down and back. Fourteen months ago."

"Mara had a full scrubber rig and a surface line that held," Wren said. "And she came up hollow. She said so herself. *Don't send anyone down there who's already been hollowed once.*"

Sol hadn't moved. Rainwater pooled at her boots. She looked at the slate, at Salas's frozen pen, at each face in the cabin, and something in her expression hardened into the shape of a decision.

"What's in it," she said. Not a question.

Wren looked up. "Mara called it a cache. Sealed from the inside. Not on hospital plans. Service side. She kept the Caller lit so somebody would come and open it."

"Pre-drown currency," Salas said. His voice was rust on metal, unused for months. He still didn't look up from his berth book. "Mercy General was a federal reserve depot before the water rose. Cold storage for the old mint's overflow. Gold. Platinum. The coins that didn't melt."

The cabin went quiet enough to hear the storm bell's pause stretching thin.

"How much?" Sol asked.

Salas's pen tapped once against the page. A single dot of ink. "Enough to buy every berth on the high ground. Enough to burn Dey's indenture clean and still have change for the Marrow's bond."

Dey made a sound — not a laugh, not a cough, something caught between. "My papers come due at the next tide. Quill won't wait."

"Quill's book is shut," Bayo said. "Count's full. She told us that herself."

"Then we make the count change," Sol said. She said it flat, no bravado, no pleading. "We bring up what's in that cache. We pay the berths. We burn the papers. We keep the boat."

"At sixty-one meters," Wren said. "Past the Line. With a scrubber canister that dies at thirty meters. With Dey's lungs rattling like a loose bolt. With Salas hollow. With Nia the only one small enough for the service trunk."

She laid it out clean, the way she always did. Facts first. Feelings after, if there was time.

"The drum has maybe two pulls left before the cable frays through," she continued. "The surge is running early. Bayo called it. The gate seals in forty minutes, maybe less. We have one shot. One diver. One line. And whatever's down there has been sitting under twelve meters of pressure and cold for fourteen months. It might be crushed. It might be gone. It might be a trap Mara set because she was already hollow and didn't know it."

She stopped. Breathed.

"Two plays left on the slate," she said. "One of them is my voice. I don't know what I said. The other —" She glanced at Salas. "— might be yours."

Sol's eyes moved to the slate. To the companionway where the storm bell hammered three strikes again, closer now, the pause almost gone.

"Play the second," she said.

Wren's thumb was already going for the actuator. Sol reached across the chart table and pressed two fingers flat on the slate's housing, pinning it.

"Leave it," she said. "We're not sitting in a cabin for forty minutes while a drowned woman talks us out of the only money on this coast. Rig the drum. We're going down the second seal on this tide. Now, before the surge puts the Stair under and the teeth shut the channel till spring."

Nobody moved. The bell hammered three and held its pause.

"Now," Sol said again, and Dey laughed, and the laugh came apart in his chest and bent him over the table. He got a hand on the edge and hung there until it passed. When he straightened there was a wet shine on his lip. He looked at his thumb, then wiped it on his trousers.

"Sure," he said. "Put me in the trunk. I'll fit if you grease me."

"You'd fit," Wren said. "You'd stall at ten meters with a heart going like a sparrow and then somebody would have to come down after you, and there's nobody left up here to do it."

"Then who," Sol said.

"Sixty-one meters," Bayo said from the hatch, bandages tucked up under his arms. "Nobody's got a canister that—"

"Her gauge reads off the hospital datum," Wren said. "Mercy's stair gauges were zeroed to the old sub-basement floor, not harbor mean. Sixty-one on her dial is thirty-eight, thirty-nine on ours, give or take whatever silt's shifted through since. Thirty-eight is still past the Line. It's still more than Dey's lungs and it's still past the canister."

The canister — the scrubber, the cartridge that pulls carbon dioxide back out of a diver's rebreathed air so they can stay under — was good to thirty meters. Everyone aboard knew the number the way they knew their own berth.

"Eight meters of dead water at the bottom," Dey said. "On a line. In the dark."

"So somebody holds a breath for a minute," Sol said. "I've done worse for less."

"You don't remember if you have." Wren said it quietly, which was worse.

Rain ran off Sol's oilskin onto the deck plates. She didn't blink and she didn't answer, and she didn't let go of the slate either.

Nia set Teo down on the deck plate. She crouched, unlaced her boots, and set them side by side against the bulkhead, toes to the wall, the way you do on a boat so you find them again in the dark.

"Hold him," she said, and Wren took the boy's weight. He weighed nothing. His fingers found her sleeve and knotted there.

"I did thirty-eight on one breath twice a day for a year," Nia said. "Cold-box to the stair and back, because there was nobody to hold a line for me and I wasn't going to ask. Give me the harness."

"You're a kid," Dey said.

"I'm the kid who kept him alive by hand." Nia didn't raise her voice. "What did you do this year, cough?"

Salas turned a page in the berth book. He didn't look up.

"Eight meters," Nia said. "My mother did thirty-eight with no line and no canister and a hole in her chest, and she didn't come up. She put us in the box and she stayed with the light. She sent us up." She stood there in her socks on the cold plate, small, absolutely steady. "So somebody had to come back down. It's me. I'm going."

Dey took the harness off its hook and held it open at the bottom, the way you hold trousers for a child. Chest strap, two thigh loops, a steel D-ring at the sternum where the ascent line clips. Nia stepped in and lifted her arms and let him cinch the cam buckle down.

"This is stupid," he said. "You'll crack your head on the dog door and I'll have to explain it to your brother."

"Teo's seen me come up out of the cold-box four hundred times." She rolled her shoulders to settle the straps. "He knows the drill."

Wren had to set the boy down to run the tape, and he came along gripping her cuff. She'd measured Mara's service hatch twice off the recording: a sixty-centimeter dog door, six lugs, wheel in the middle. Forty-six across Nia's shoulders with the harness on. She said both numbers out loud so nobody could claim later they hadn't heard them.

"Sixty," Dey said. "Fine. Then I'm on the drum."

"You're not diving."

"I'm not sitting dry on deck while a kid goes down for *my* papers." He had the tag line in his fist — the light line that stops a diver spinning on the wire — wound around his knuckles too tight. "Put me on the line. I'll hold my breath the whole way down."

"You'd stall at ten meters and I'd be under you with no third option," Nia said. "No."

"You don't get a vote. You're nine."

"I'm the one going."

Sol came in through the hatch with rain sheeting off her oilskin. "Dey on the drum. Wren on the wire, you feel a diver through a line better than anyone aboard. Bayo—"

"Bow," Bayo said. "Somebody watches the Stair mouth."

"Your hands are in your armpits."

"They work."

Nobody looked at him when he said it. Wren put the crank handle into Dey's hands and closed his fingers round it, and he let her, which was its own kind of answer.

The drum was a spool of eleven-millimeter wire on a bolted frame, geared down so one man could crank a hundred kilos up out of the water, with a toothed pawl for a brake that ticked once per link. Two good pulls left before the strands fuzzed at the fairlead. She'd said that already. She said it again, because the tide was in the cabin with them now, sucking at the hull.

Dey's indenture lay on the chart table under a shackle so the spray wouldn't take it. Wren read the date off it upside down and said nothing. The current had turned. The Marrow had come off her lines and was lying back against them, and the debris in the channel had stopped running one way and started going nowhere at all.

"Who's got the boat," Wren said.

"I've got the boat."

"That's not a name. You'll be on the drum or the line or in the trunk, so who's got the wheel."

"I've got the boat," Sol said again, and put her hand flat on the wheel housing like she was holding it shut.

"Fine. Then tell me what's behind that seal. You didn't get it off a fourteen-month-old tape. Tell me."

Sol looked at her a moment. "It's dogged from the inside. Bring a pry bar, not a key."

Rain came through the hatch. Nobody filled the space after that, and Sol didn't either. She moved her hand a half turn on the housing and left it there.

"Surge is early," Bayo called from the bow. "Water's over the gate's lower lip — I can see it going green across the sill. Bell's not waiting on us."

Wren went out along the deck with Teo on her hip and the slate pinched under her arm, and put her palm flat on the wire where it left the fairlead. Nothing yet, just cold. Then the pawl ticked once as Dey took up the slack, and Nia sat down on the rail with her bare feet hooked inboard, forty-six centimeters of kid and a sixty-centimeter door waiting at the bottom.

The swell came out of the channel's shoulder, not the bow — a wall of gray water that had been building all night behind the gate's teeth and decided now was its hour. It hit the Marrow broadside with a sound like a freight container dropped from a crane. The hull shuddered. Lines snapped taut with pistol-crack reports. Wren's boots slid on the wet deck plate, Teo yelped against her chest, and the slate flew from her arm in a slow, stupid arc.

She caught it one-handed against her ribs. The actuator was depressed. The spool was turning.

Static hissed, then a voice — low, clear, cutting through the storm and the bell and the creak of the Marrow's ribs — spoke from the speaker.

*"This is Wren Achebe, reader, Marrow. Time stamp fourteen months, three days, zero-six hundred hours. I am at the pharmacy hatch, thirty-nine meters on the hospital gauge. Salas is on the line above me. Vos is below, at the second seal. I am recording this because I have been ordered to record this, and because if I do not record it I will not remember that I was here."*

Wren's fingers froze on the housing. The voice was hers. The cadence, the breath between clauses, the way she swallowed the *r* in *ordered* — hers. But the words had never passed her lips. Fourteen months ago she had been on the high ground, in the arcology's archive level, rebuilding slates for divers who came up hollow. She had never been on the Marrow. She had never been thirty-nine meters down.

*"Vos reports the second seal is dogged from the inside. No external wheel. She requires a pry bar and two minutes of work at sixty-one meters. Salas has the bar. He is descending now. I am holding the tag line. The current is running three knots across the trunk mouth. If Salas stalls, I cut him loose. That is the order. That is the only order."*

The recording went on. Wren stood on the heaving deck, Teo clutching her sleeve, the storm bell hammering three strikes and not pausing this time, and listened to herself condemn a man to death in a voice she did not know.

*"Salas is at the seal. He has the bar. He is working. His breath is ragged. He is past the Line. His gauge reads fifty-eight meters and climbing. I am telling him to come up. He is not coming up. He says the seal is turning. He says — "*

A sound on the tape. Metal on metal. A grunt, wet and surprised. Then Salas's voice, thin with pressure: *"Got it. Coming up. Wren — "*

*"Salas, ascend. Now. That is an order."*

*"Wren, the cache — "*

*"Ascend. I will cut the line at sixty seconds."*

*"The cache is — "*

The tape ate the rest. Static roared. The actuator clicked back to neutral, mechanical and final.

Wren stared at the slate. Her thumb found the play counter through salt crust. *One play left.*

Behind her, the companionway framed Nia on the rail, harness clipped, bare feet hooked inboard. Dey's hand on the crank. Bayo's bandaged fists on the bow rail. Sol's palm on the wheel housing, white-knuckled, not moving.

The Marrow rolled. The wire sang once as the pawl caught.

Wren's mouth moved, but the wind took the words.
